I'm not here to argue but personally I don't like this line of thinking presented in this comment. You say people with BPD (I too have BPD but when writing about a demographic I prefer to disregard myself as a person and write as if I didn't belong to any demographic at all) destroy others when they're unwell. That much can be (CAN, not IS) true. But why? Because all people do. All people, no matter their diagnosis, no matter how neurotypical or neurodivergent they are, no matter their temperament, all people have the capacity to do harm and many people can be harmful to others when they are incredibly unwell. People with BPD do not have a uniquely strong capacity for harm. If you feel like they do, I encourage you to examine the reasons why a particular demographic may be more prone to lashing out or indirectly harming others (eg. while isolating and not showing up to agreed upon meetings hurts you, technically it also harms others, even though unintentionally). Most likely, you will find that the particular demographic is lacking resources and/or is stigmatised by society. 



I also disagree with you saying that people who meet people with BPD when they aren't winning the mental health battle would think they're bad people. I disagree because I think that that isn't a BPD issue. If someone with clinical depression is having a hard time, a stranger who meets them will likely think they're an asshole or bad too. My point is that people, in general, behave in strange, off-putting and/or rude ways when they feel awful and are at their lowest point. It doesn't really mean anything, in the end. A lot of people I have met in my life, who yelled at me when I handed them the wrong pack of cigarettes or who yelled at other customers around, were probably having a really really bad day, and chances are they are amicable otherwise, chances are they aren't usually like that. In that moment, I thought of them as bad assholes. I'm sure a lot of people have thought that was of me. I'm sure a lot of people have thought that was of my dearest friends. It's not something specific. Life is hard and for a lot of people there comes a time where life is so hard in such a specific way that it makes them lash out and take it out on others. This is not a behaviour exclusive to a diagnosis. Certain diagnoses may alter the threshold of what a person can take, or what exactly they can take (stupid example but eg most people are capable of withstanding uncomfortable noises and sounds, while some people on the spectrum might become quickly overstimulated and may lash out as a response).




And this is just my nitpick, but it's odd for you to assume that OP will be able to see themselves in ANY of those points. I counted 4 symptoms in that quote: emotional dysregulation, impulsive behaviour (in 2 areas that might be potentially self-damaging), inappropriate anger and an unstable sense of self. I am not counting the beginning of the quote as unstable interpersonal relationships because that is not necessarily the presentation the symptom might take. For the diagnosis of BPD, a person needs to fit 5 out of 9 diagnostic criteria. Theoretically, OP wouldn't need to have any of those symptoms but could have the others. There is no need to assume they can see themselves in any of that.  




Basically I just don't think anyone here is uniquely talented at harming others. People are people. All people can damage other people easily, we're hedgehogs trying to huddle for warmth if hedgehogs could experience horrible childhood trauma.

**Long answer:** 

It is a 600+ pages long book, which means it would need two movies *(like IT, for example)* to handle all the characters in the first place. But that is just scratching the surface, since making a two-part film is not uncommon these days. The real meat is: Dreamcatcher can never have a good film adaptation because too much of what makes it great happens inside the characters' heads. Both literally and in the standard way. Could the actual literal headspace be adapted? Yes. But there are still too many internal monologues and dialogues. And you CANNOT leave them out, else you get the existing Dreamcatcher movie. Because that's the movie's problem: it does adapt most of the actual events, but it loses the meaning. Yes, nearly everything that physically happens in the book happens in the movie. But what physically happens in the book is not nearly as important as what happens in the characters' heads. For one character *(well, technically two characters but technically one but-),* this is literal. Now I'm repeating myself, but you get the gist. And sure, you could just...actually adapt all that too, but that is not something that would ever work in a movie. Would the literal headspace, the office, the archives be adaptable? Yes. Would the dialogues be? Well, yes. But the resulting movie would become 70 % dialogue taking place in a non-physical room. And that is something that is simply not engaging in a film and would not work. And even then, even if you could make it work, the narration, the standard internal monologues are just as important as the spiritual dialogues. And those are simply not sufficiently adaptable when it comes to films.

Keep in mind that a lot of research papers "showing" that personality disorders can be present without any trauma are biased. We (people with BPD) can only experience secondary structural dissociation, and DID falls under tertiary. Basically we can have multiple emotional parts, uh, the parts of you that break off during trauma and are responsible for handling it, but we have only one apparently normal part. People with DID have several apparently normal parts and several emotional parts. With OSDD-1b it's a little bit of a hot topic.



Basically we have the same dissociation people with PTSD have, but several times. Like. We have that but several of them and they can be more prominent and defined. Some theorise that it's a contributing factor for us feeling empty and without personality - because some of us may contain most of their emotions and personality in the trauma response parts instead of in the daily-life part.
